questions.text:
The Glossary manager wants to boost the basket value and reduce missed cross-sell opportunities. The manager believes that certain items, such as milk, bread, cheese, butter, eggs, bananas, and coffee, are frequently bought together; these items should be co-located on the shelves. For this scenario, apply the Apriori algorithm to verify that buying patterns are interesting to the users.

Consider the following transaction logs shown in Table Q.1A.

| TID | Items |
|---|---|
| T1 | milk, bread, egg |
| T2 | milk, bread, banana |
| T3 | milk, cheese, banana |
| T4 | bread, butter, cheese |
| T5 | milk, bread, butter, cheese |
| T6 | milk, coffee, bread |
| T7 | banana, cheese |
| T8 | milk, bread, egg, butter |
| T9 | milk, bread, cheese |
| T10 | coffee, bread |

Answer the followings (candidate set represented as C, Frequent itemset represented as L):

i. Build C₁ → L₁, C₂ → L₂, C₃ → L₃ with min support count = 4; list pruned candidates at each stage.

ii. Generate rules from the largest Lk with min_conf = 70%; compute support, confidence. If min_sup changes to 5, which itemsets drop? Briefly explain via the Apriori property.
questions.approach: Count singletons, join frequent itemsets to form larger candidates, and prune any candidate with an infrequent subset before checking support. From the largest frequent itemsets, calculate rule support as joint count divided by transaction count and confidence as joint count divided by antecedent count. Reapply the changed support threshold to the retained counts.

questions.text: A medical equipment company claims that its new blood test kit has an average accuracy rate of 95%. A quality inspector believes the true accuracy may be different from the claimed value (it could be higher or lower). To verify the claim, a random sample of 36 test kits is taken, and the sample shows an average accuracy of 94.7% with a known population standard deviation of 0.02. At the 5% significance level, test whether the company's claim is justified. (critical z-values are ±1.96)
questions.approach: State a null mean equal to the claim and a two-sided alternative, then calculate z = (sample mean − claimed mean)/(σ/√n) and compare it with the supplied critical bounds. Put the mean and standard deviation on the same scale before substitution: the paper does not specify whether its standard deviation is in proportion units or percentage points.

questions.text: An ice cream manufacturer noticed that sales of ice cream increase every summer and drop in winter. The sales pattern repeats each year with increasing average sales overtime due to marketing efforts. Which components are present in this time series? Identify the time series model that would best represent this pattern and why?
questions.approach: Separate long-term movement from recurring calendar patterns, then consider an additive or multiplicative component model. Check whether seasonal amplitude stays constant or grows with the series level; the question does not specify that feature, so state the assumption used to choose a model.

questions.text:
Table Q. 2A shown below has the data collected during the outbreak of smallpox.

| Group | Attacked | Not attacked | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vaccinated | 31 | 469 | 500 |
| Not Vaccinated | 185 | 1315 | 1500 |
| Total | 216 | 1784 | 2000 |

Test the effectiveness of vaccination in preventing smallpox at 5% significance level.
questions.approach: Form expected cell counts from row total × column total / grand total, then calculate χ² = Σ(O−E)²/E with degrees of freedom (rows−1)(columns−1). Check the expected-count assumptions, compare with the significance-level cutoff, and examine group attack proportions to describe the direction of any association.

questions.text:
Consider frequent 1-itemsets:

L₁ = {A, B, C, D, E, F}.

Use the hash function

h(x,y) = ((order(x) × 5) + order(y)) mod 7

and the following transactions:

- T₁: {A, B, C}
- T₂: {A, D, E}
- T₃: {B, C, E, F}
- T₄: {A, B, E, F}.

i. Construct the hash table H₂ showing bucket addresses, counts, and contents.

ii. If the minimum support is 4, which buckets can be pruned?
questions.approach: State an item-order convention, enumerate each unordered pair in every transaction, and apply the supplied hash function while counting repeated occurrences and collisions. Prune buckets below the support threshold, then distinguish surviving buckets from genuinely frequent pairs. Treat the stated frequent-singleton set as supplied for the exercise, since its label is inconsistent with the logs at the stated threshold.

questions.text:
Two forecasting models for production planning are evaluated as follows:

| Model | MAE | MSE | RMSE | MAPE |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Model A | 12 | 25 | 5 | 6% |
| Model B | 10 | 36 | 6 | 4% |

Justify and explain which model gives better overall forecasting performance? Explain, considering all measures.
questions.approach: Compare absolute-error, squared-error, and percentage-error measures against the forecasting objective rather than treating them as interchangeable votes. First check metric consistency: for the same errors and scale, RMSE must be at least MAE, but the printed table violates this inequality in both rows.

questions.text:
i. Find the standard deviation and skewness for the following data:

78, 91, 68, 54, 82, 47, 60, 78, 97, 58, 62, 50, 50, 63, 92, 75 79, 63, 42, 61

ii. Give example for "Combining variables" concept in dataset preparation.

iii. A CMO of a company marketing carbonated soft drinks has developed three new flavors of cola and decided to measure the customers' preference for these three flavors from 12 customers by using scale of 1 to 9. The table of data is shown below. Conduct the appropriate analysis here.

| Flavor-A | Flavor-B | Flavor-C |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | 6 | 8 |
| 2 | 4 | 6 |
| 4 | 5 | 8 |
| 2 | 5 | 6 |
questions.method: Descriptive statistics, derived variables, and one-way ANOVA
questions.approach: For part (i), state the sample/population and skewness conventions, compute centered deviations, and resolve the missing separator between adjacent observations in the printed list. For part (ii), describe deriving a new column from existing variables; for part (iii), compare between-group and within-group mean squares using one-way ANOVA if the flavor ratings come from independent groups. State a significance level and the independence assumption, since the paper leaves them unspecified.

questions.text:
A dataset contains 100 transactions.

- 20 transactions include both {Pen, Notebook}.
- 25 transactions include {Pen}.
- 40 transactions include {Notebook}.

i. Calculate Support and Confidence for the rule {Pen} → {Notebook}.

ii. If the minimum support is 10% and minimum confidence is 60%, check whether the rule is strong.

iii. Interpret the result.
questions.approach: Calculate support as joint transaction count divided by total count and confidence as joint count divided by antecedent count. Compare each measure with its own threshold and interpret the two denominators distinctly, without treating association as causation.

questions.text:
Consider the sales for the past 5 weeks: 120, 130, 125, 140, 150.

i. Compute the 3-week Simple Moving Average (SMA) forecast for week 6.

ii. Comment briefly on the difference between the SMA and WMA forecasts.
questions.approach: Average the actual observations in the requested trailing window to obtain the next-period SMA. Contrast equal weighting with WMA weights that sum to unity; the paper supplies no WMA weights, so restrict that comparison to the method rather than inventing a numerical WMA.

questions.text:
Given the following transaction database:

| TID | Items |
|---|---|
| 1 | A, C |
| 2 | A, B, D |
| 3 | A, B, C |
| 4 | B, C, D |
| 5 | A, C |

a) Convert the above database into vertical data format and find all frequent itemsets with a minimum support of 2.

b) List the advantages of using vertical data format over horizontal format in frequent itemset mining?
questions.approach: Build a transaction-ID set for each item, then intersect sets to obtain the support counts of larger itemsets. Retain sets meeting minimum support and stop extending branches that fail it. Discuss the trade-off between reusable set intersections and repeated horizontal database scans.

questions.text:
A company tracks monthly sales (in units) for a product:

| Month | Sales |
|---|---|
| 1 | 120 |
| 2 | 135 |
| 3 | 150 |
| 4 | 160 |
| 5 | 170 |

Using Single Exponential Smoothing (SES) with a smoothing constant α = 0.3, and assuming the forecast for Month 1 is 120 units,

(a) Calculate the forecast for Months 2 to 6.

(b) Compute the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) for the forecasts from Months 2 to 5.
questions.approach: Starting from the given initial forecast, update F(t+1) = αY(t) + (1−α)F(t) sequentially without rounding intermediate forecasts. Align each forecast with its actual value in the requested evaluation period, then average the absolute errors; exclude any future period without an observed value.

questions.text:
A supermarket's market-basket analysis generates several association rules, such as:

- Rule 1: Diapers → Beer (support = 5%, confidence = 80%)
- Rule 2: Milk → Bread (support = 20%, confidence = 60%)

Some rules may appear strong based on support and confidence but can be misleading.

a. Explain why some association rules can be misleading even if they have high support and confidence.

b. Identify at least two additional measures that can be used to evaluate the true strength of a rule.
questions.approach: Examine how a common consequent can inflate confidence, then compare joint occurrence with the individual item frequencies. Consider measures such as lift, Kulczynski, or cosine and identify the marginal supports each requires; the supplied rule summaries alone do not provide all those inputs.

questions.text:
A transportation company tracks its monthly passenger counts (Yt). The data for the first five months are given. Applying Holt's Method

| Period | Month | Passenger Count |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Jan | 400 |
| 2 | Feb | 450 |
| 3 | Mar | 520 |
| 4 | Apr | 500 |
| 5 | May | 550 |

Parameters: Use smoothing constants

a. Calculate the initial Level (L1) and Trend (T2).

b. Calculate the final Level (L5) and Trend (T5) based on all five data points.

c. Use L5 and T5 to provide the forecast for Month 7 (F7).
questions.subtopic: Holt initialization, recursion, and missing parameters
questions.approach: State an initialization convention using the initial observation and first difference, then update the level and trend before projecting by the forecast horizon. The paper omits both smoothing constants α and β, so give the recurrence symbolically and request those parameters before attempting numerical final states or forecasts. Clarify the initial-trend indexing used in the question.

questions.text:
An online electronics store analysed 1,000 customer purchase transactions. The following data were obtained:

| Itemset | Number of Transactions |
|---|---|
| {Smartphone} | 420 |
| {Wireless Earbuds} | 380 |
| {Smartphone, Wireless Earbuds} | 260 |

(a) Calculate the pattern evaluation measures such as Lift, Kulc and cosine for the following association rule:

Smartphone → WirelessEarbuds

(b) Justify the relationship between Smartphone and Earbud purchases based on the obtained Lift and Kulc values.
questions.approach: Convert joint and marginal counts into supports, then compute lift = P(A∩B)/(P(A)P(B)), Kulc = [P(B|A)+P(A|B)]/2, and cosine = P(A∩B)/√[P(A)P(B)]. Interpret lift against the independence baseline and Kulc as an average of directional confidences, without assigning it a universal independence cutoff.

questions.text:
A data analyst is studying the annual income levels (in ₹000s) of 12 employees in a company:

[180, 200, 210, 215, 220, 230, 250, 270, 300, 320, 400, 480]

Apply both equal-width and equal-frequency binning with 3 bins.

Using histogram analysis, discuss which binning approach (equal-width or equal-frequency) provides a better representation of the income distribution and justify your reasoning.
questions.approach: Sort the incomes, divide the full range by the requested number of bins for equal-width boundaries, and split the ordered observations into balanced groups for equal-frequency bins. State boundary-inclusion rules, then compare how each scheme represents concentration and the upper tail. For unequal-width histogram bins, use frequency density so bar area represents frequency.

questions.text:
(a) A mobile accessories retailer analyses six recent online orders to understand attachment behaviour around new smartphone purchases. The transaction log are shown in Table Q.1A.

The product codes map to real items as follows: a = Smartphone; b = Protective Case; c = Screen Protector; d = Power Bank; e = USB Cable.

| Transaction ID | Items |
| --- | --- |
| T1 | a, b, d, e |
| T2 | b, c, e |
| T3 | a, b, d, e |
| T4 | a, b, c, e |
| T5 | a, b, c, d, e |
| T6 | b, c, d |

(b) Derive all possible frequent k-itemsets with minimum support count=3 and following the Apriori property, list pruned itemsets at each stage.

(c) Generate a minimum of 5 possible association rules using the longest frequent k-itemsets and verify whether the generated rules are strong with the confidence threshold=60%.
questions.subtopic: Frequent itemsets and strong association rules
questions.approach: Count singleton supports, join frequent sets level by level, and prune any candidate with an infrequent subset before counting its support. From the longest frequent sets, form rules with nonempty disjoint antecedents and consequents; check minimum support and confidence using count(antecedent ∪ consequent) / count(antecedent).

questions.text: A hospital laboratory claims that a new COVID testing kit correctly identifies infection 95% of the time. A researcher believes that the true accuracy is less than 95% and decides to test this claim at a 5% significance level. A random sample of n = 50 test results gives a sample mean accuracy of 0.93. The population standard deviation is known to be 0.04. At the 5% significance level, test whether the hospital laboratory's claim is justified. (critical value Z_{0.05}=-1.645).
questions.subtopic: Testing a mean with known population standard deviation
questions.approach: Set the null mean to the claimed accuracy and use a lower-tailed alternative. Follow the paper's supplied known-standard-deviation model: calculate z = (sample mean − null mean) / (population standard deviation / √n), compare it with the stated critical value, and express the decision in context.

questions.text: Consider the scenario of mobile phone sales data, the mobile phone retailer analyzed monthly sales data over the period of 3 years. The data showed consistent upward movement due to market growth, with a little drop due to global electronic chip shortages. Identify the component of time series that represents the market growth, and name the time series component denote temporary drop?
questions.subtopic: Trend, seasonality, cyclicality and irregular variation
questions.approach: Distinguish sustained long-run movement from fixed seasonal repetition, multi-year cycles, and isolated external shocks. Classify each described movement by its duration and whether it recurs regularly.

questions.text:
Per acre production data (in tons) for three varieties of wheat grown using four different fertilizers, each combination replicated twice, are given in Table Q. 2A. Test whether the variety differences and fertilizer differences are significant at 5% level.

| Variety | Replicate | Fertilizer 1 | Fertilizer 2 | Fertilizer 3 | Fertilizer 4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Variety 1 | 1 | 8 | 9 | 6 | 10 |
| Variety 1 | 2 | 9 | 8 | 7 | 11 |
| Variety 2 | 1 | 7 | 8 | 5 | 9 |
| Variety 2 | 2 | 6 | 9 | 4 | 10 |
| Variety 3 | 1 | 10 | 11 | 8 | 12 |
| Variety 3 | 2 | 9 | 12 | 7 | 13 |
questions.approach: Calculate grand, factor and cell means, then partition total variation into variety, fertilizer, interaction and within-cell error sums of squares. Divide each sum by its degrees of freedom, compare each main-effect mean square with the within-cell error mean square, and use the appropriate F critical values under the independent, normal, equal-variance error assumptions.

Order each pair consistently, hash every pair occurrence using the supplied function, and sum counts by bucket. Prune buckets below minimum support and retain their complement's pairs as candidates, then distinguish bucket counts from exact pair supports; the supplied singleton set is inconsistent with the stated support threshold, so explicitly state whether you follow that supplied premise.

questions.text:
Differentiate between Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Mean Squared Error (MSE). Assume two model with given MAE and RMSE. Interpret the results and identify the better forecasting model. Justify your answer briefly.

- Model A: MAE = 5.2, RMSE = 6.8
- Model B: MAE = 4.9, RMSE = 5.0
questions.approach: Define MAE as the mean absolute error and MSE as the mean squared error; relate RMSE to the square root of MSE. Compare the reported measures on the same evaluation data and scale, noting that squared-error measures give greater weight to large errors.

questions.text:
i) Find the elements of box plot using the following data: 78, 91, 68, 54, 82, 47, 60, 78, 97, 58, 62, 50, 50, 63, 92, 75 79, 63, 42, 61.

ii) Why is it sometimes necessary to create subsets from a large dataset before performing analysis?

iii) Measure the strength of the relationship between the ranks assigned by two different interviewers as shown below.

| Candidate | Interviewer 1 | Interviewer 2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 1 | 1 |
| B | 2 | 2 |
| C | 3 | 4 |

| G | 7 | 8 |
| H | 8 | 7 |
| I | 9 | 10 |
| J | 10 | 9 |

Transcription note: the paper omits the comma in “75 79”; these are treated as separate observations.
questions.subtopic: Quartiles, data subsets and rank association
questions.method: Box plot and Spearman rank correlation
questions.approach: Sort the observations, state a quartile convention, and use the interquartile range to set Tukey fences and identify whiskers or outliers; treat the printed “75 79” as two observations and disclose the missing comma. Explain the purpose and representativeness of subsetting, then compute rank differences and use Spearman's no-ties formula, ρ = 1 − 6Σd² / [n(n² − 1)].

Count transactions containing each requested itemset and divide by the total transaction count. Apply the support threshold, then examine each frequent itemset's proper supersets to distinguish frequency from maximal frequency.

questions.text: The sales of a retail store for five consecutive weeks are as follows: 100, 110, 95, 120, 130. Compute the 3-week moving average forecast for week 6. Interpret the whether this method would be appropriate if a strong upward trend continues.
questions.approach: Average the most recent observations in the stated window to forecast the next period, without using an unknown future actual. Explain whether averaging past levels can follow a continuing trend and compare its behavior with a trend-aware method.

questions.text:
Given the following transaction database:

| TID | Items |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | A, B, D |
| 2 | B, C, E |
| 3 | A, B, C, E |
| 4 | B, E |

(a) Using the FP-Growth algorithm, mine all frequent itemsets with a minimum support of 2.

- Construct the FP-tree.
- Show the conditional pattern bases and conditional FP-trees.
- List all frequent itemsets.

(b) State the advantages of the pattern growth approach over the Apriori algorithm.
questions.approach: Remove infrequent singleton items, order the retained items consistently by support, and insert ordered transactions into an FP-tree with shared-prefix counts. For each suffix, construct its counted conditional pattern base and conditional tree, recursively grow frequent patterns, and explain how this avoids Apriori's explicit candidate generation.

questions.text:
A beverage company tracks monthly sales (in units) of a new energy drink:

| Month | Sales |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | 80 |
| 2 | 95 |
| 3 | 100 |
| 4 | 110 |
| 5 | 120 |

Using Single Exponential Smoothing (SES) with a smoothing constant α=0.4, and assuming the forecast for Month 1 = 80 units,

(a) Calculate the forecast for Months 2 to 6.

(b) Compute the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) for the forecasts from Months 2 to 5.
questions.approach: Starting from the given initial forecast, repeatedly apply F(next) = α × actual(current) + (1 − α) × forecast(current), retaining precision between steps. Compute MAE only over the requested periods with both a forecast and an observed actual.

questions.text:
A popular online bookstore analysed 800 customer purchase transactions and obtained the following data:

| Itemset | Number of Transactions |
| --- | --- |
| {Fiction Book} | 360 |
| {E-Reader} | 300 |
| {Fiction Book, E-Reader} | 180 |

(a) Calculate the pattern evaluation measures Lift and Kulc for the association rule: Fiction Book → E-Reader.

(b) Interpret what the obtained Lift and Kulc values indicate about the relationship between Fiction Book and E-Reader purchases.
questions.approach: Convert the item and co-occurrence counts into supports, then compute lift as joint support divided by the product of marginal supports. Compute Kulczynski as the average of the two directional confidences, and interpret the measures against their reference values without inferring causation.

questions.text:
A manufacturing unit tracks its quarterly production output. The data for the first four quarters are given below:

| Period (t) | Actual Production (Yt) |
| --- | --- |
| Q1 | 100 |
| Q2 | 120 |
| Q3 | 130 |
| Q4 | 150 |

Use smoothing constants =0.2 and =0.4. Applying Holt's Method

(a) Calculate the initial Level (L1) and Trend (T2).

(b) Calculate the Level (L2) and Trend (T3) for periods 2 and 3, respectively.

(c) Calculate the Forecast for period 4 (F4).

(d) Differentiate between Double and triple exponential smoothing techniques.

Transcription note: the paper omits the names of the smoothing constants and uses inconsistent trend subscripts. State the convention used.
questions.subtopic: Level and trend updates with initialization assumptions
questions.approach: The paper omits the smoothing-parameter labels and uses inconsistent initial-trend subscripts, so explicitly state which constant updates level, which updates trend, and how you initialize and index the states. Update level and trend sequentially, forecast from the latest available states without using the target period's actual, and explain the seasonal component added by triple exponential smoothing.

questions.text:
A transaction database is given as follows:

| Transaction ID | Items Purchased |
| --- | --- |
| T1 | A, B, C |
| T2 | A, C, D |
| T3 | B, C, E |
| T4 | A, B, C, E |
| T5 | A, B, D, E |

(a) List all frequent itemsets having minimum support = 2.

(b) Identify the closed frequent itemsets and maximal frequent itemsets from the result.

(c) Explain why mining closed and max patterns is more efficient than mining all frequent itemsets.
questions.approach: Enumerate itemsets meeting the support-count threshold. Test closedness by checking for a proper superset with equal support and maximality by checking for any frequent proper superset, then explain the different information retained by these compact pattern representations.

questions.text: A data scientist is analysing the following cholesterol level (mg/dL) readings of 12 patients: [145, 155, 160, 162, 165, 172, 180, 190, 200, 220, 240, 260]. Apply equal-width and equal-frequency binning with 3 bins. Using histogram analysis, explain which binning approach (width-based or frequency-based) better represents the data distribution and why.
questions.approach: For equal-width bins, divide the observed range by the requested bin count and state endpoint-inclusion rules; for equal-frequency bins, sort the data and split observations into similarly sized groups. Compare how their histograms show concentration and skew, remembering that unequal-width bins require density rather than raw count heights for comparable areas.
